summary: This informational RFC discusses IPv6 Neighbor Discovery problems arising from huge /64 subnets. Simple implementations can suffer denial of service when scans create large numbers of cache entries. It describes issues and mitigations.

plainLanguage.summary: A huge empty street means a delivery person can waste time knocking on doors that do not exist. This explains how that can overload routers and what to do.

questions: why can ipv6 neighbor discovery be attacked
how to protect a router from ndp exhaustion
what is the problem with ipv6 /64 subnets
subtitle: How huge IPv6 subnets let a network scan or an attacker overwhelm a router's Neighbor Discovery, and what to do about it.

tldr.problem: The default IPv6 subnet is a /64, so scanning it makes a router try to resolve addresses for huge numbers of hosts that do not exist, which can exhaust its Neighbor Discovery capacity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how the forwarding plane hands unresolved destinations to the control plane through a queue, then lists operator mitigations (filtering, small subnets, routing tricks, queue rate tuning) and advice for implementors (prioritize, tune queues).
tldr.outcome: Operators get workarounds the RFC itself calls kludges, and vendors get guidance to build more robust Neighbor Discovery implementations.

today: RFC 6583 is Informational and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on the Neighbor Discovery protocol in RFC 4861.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
In IPv4, subnets are generally just large enough for the machines on them; an IPv4 /20 holds only 4096 addresses. The default IPv6 subnet is a /64, which covers literally billions of billions of addresses, nearly all unassigned. A simplistic Neighbor Discovery (ND) implementation can fail when it tries to resolve large numbers of those unassigned addresses.

The trigger can be a deliberate denial-of-service attack or a legitimate scanning tool used for inventory or security audits. When probes arrive via a router for a directly attached network, the router creates Neighbor Cache entries that stay INCOMPLETE and never complete, overwhelming its capacity, exhausting memory and pushing out in-use mappings. The consequences listed are that new devices may be unable to join a network, new IPv6 flows may be impossible to establish and existing flows may be interrupted. The RFC notes that the DoS caused by scanning was previously described in RFC 5157, and that some routers rate-limit Neighbor Solicitations, which helps but does not fully fix it.
sections.plainLanguage: A scanner asks about every house number on a giant street. The router writes each one down and waits for an answer that never comes, until it has no room left for the real houses.

sections.title: How Routers Handle Address Resolution
sections.content:
Modern routers separate the forwarding plane, usually hardware, from the control plane, mostly software on a general purpose processor. To deliver a packet to a neighbor on an attached link, the forwarding plane checks the Neighbor Cache for a link-layer address. If none exists, it puts a request in a queue and signals the Neighbor Discovery Process (NDP) in the control plane.

Per RFC 4861, the device creates a Neighbor Cache Entry in the INCOMPLETE state, queues the packet, sends one or more Neighbor Solicitations and completes the entry when a Neighbor Advertisement arrives. The same process also handles maintenance such as Neighbor Unreachability Detection.

An attacker who sends packets to many addresses on a subnet can fill the queue with attempts to resolve unused addresses. That crowds out legitimate resolution and can stop the router maintaining existing entries or answering Neighbor Solicitations. In the RFC's testing, four simultaneous nmap sessions from a low-end computer were enough to make a router's ND process unusable, and the failure was observed across multiple platforms, including the largest router platforms available at the start of the work.
sections.plainLanguage: The fast part of the router asks a slower helper to find out who lives at each address. A flood of silly questions keeps the helper too busy to answer the important ones.

sections.title: Operational Mitigations
sections.content:
The RFC offers four options, admitting that some are kludges and hard to manage. Operators are responsible for judging their impact.

  • Filtering unused address space: address hosts into a small part of the subnet and use ACLs or null routing for the rest, for example null-routing the subnet with a more specific /122 route. This needs static or stateful addressing and may not work with stateless autoconfiguration (RFC 4862).
  • Minimal subnet sizing: size subnets to the addresses in use, such as a /127 on inter-router links as recommended in RFC 6164. Prefixes longer than a /64 cannot use stateless autoconfiguration.
  • Routing mitigation: route the subnet to a discard interface and have individual hosts announce /128 routes into the IGP. This is powerful but makes many operators uncomfortable about hosts in the IGP.
  • Tuning the NDP queue rate limit: a lower rate can make an attack succeed faster and slow learning of legitimate addresses, and is worth investigating only if resolution of unknown addresses and maintenance of existing entries use separate queues.
sections.plainLanguage: You can block the empty part of the street, build a smaller street, tell the router exactly where each house is, or limit how fast it knocks on doors. Each trick has a catch.

sections.title: Advice for Implementors
sections.content:
The RFC tells implementors to program defensively: manage resources explicitly, and prioritize. Responding to Neighbor Solicitations for one's own address matters more than starting resolution that creates new entries, and Neighbor Unreachability Detection matters more than creating entries for possibly nonexistent neighbors.

It lists activities in rough priority order, which should be configurable by the operator: first, responding to Neighbor Solicitations for the router's own addresses; second, revalidating existing in-use entries; third, ND activity for traffic the router itself sources; and lowest, traffic to unknown addresses. It suggests distinguishing never-seen addresses from those that once had an entry.

Where requests share a single queue, vendors should let operators control the request rate and the queue size, ideally per interface or per prefix with limits below the global limit. The RFC gives an example of the balance: in a datacenter with 6,000 hosts on one router, a rate under 1000 could mean over 6 seconds to resolve all addresses from an initial state.
sections.plainLanguage: Builders of routers should answer questions about the router's own address first, keep up with friends already known, and leave strangers for last.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document outlines mitigations operators can use against denial-of-service attacks. It warns that implementation advice to vendors carries the risk of previously unforeseen consequences, but says it is not believed that these mitigations, or finer-grained queuing of NDP activity, create additional security risks or DoS exposure.
sections.plainLanguage: The fixes should not open any new holes, though the authors admit they cannot be completely sure.
